units.title: Physical Quantities
topics: Dimensions and uses of dimensional analysis

sections.title: Dimensions and uses of dimensional analysis

summary: A measurement is Q = nu, and n1u1 = n2u2; SI has seven base quantities.
Accuracy = closeness to the true value; precision = closeness of repeated readings, limited by the least count.
Vernier L.C. = 1 MSD - 1 VSD; screw-gauge L.C. = pitch ÷ number of circular divisions.
Systematic errors spoil accuracy and are removed by calibration; random errors spoil precision and are reduced by averaging. Quote results as a ± Δ amean.
Significant figures = certain digits + first uncertain digit. Addition keeps the least decimal places; multiplication keeps the least significant figures.
Errors combine as Δ Z = Δ A + Δ B for sums, and Δ Z/Z = p Δ A/A + q Δ B/B for products and powers.

The principle of homogeneity says every term of a physical equation has the same dimensions. Dimensional analysis checks equations, converts units via n2 = n1 (M1/M2)^a(L1/L2)^b(T1/T2)^c, and derives simple relations.
It cannot give dimensionless constants, handle more than three variables, build equations with several terms, or separate work from torque.

units.title: Vectors
topics: Triangle, parallelogram and polygon laws of vectors

sections.title: Triangle, parallelogram and polygon laws of vectors

summary: Scalars need a magnitude only; vectors need magnitude and direction and add by the triangle, parallelogram or polygon law.
Parallelogram law: R = √P^2 + Q^2 + 2PQcosθ and tanα = Qsinθ/(P + Qcosθ). Maximum P+Q at 0^°, minimum P-Q at 180^°.
A closed polygon of vectors means zero resultant — the equilibrium condition.
Resolution: Ax = Acosθ, Ay = Asinθ; recombine with A = √Ax^2 + Ay^2, tanθ = Ay/Ax.
A = A/A; A = Axi + Ayj + Azk with A = √Ax^2 + Ay^2 + Az^2 and l^2+m^2+n^2=1.
Dot product AcdotB = ABcosθ = AxBx + AyBy + AzBz; it is a scalar and vanishes for perpendicular vectors.
Cross product AtimesB = ABsinθ n; it is a vector, vanishes for parallel vectors, reverses sign on swapping, and its magnitude is the area of the parallelogram formed by the two vectors.

units.title: Kinematics
topics: Motion of a freely falling body

sections.title: Motion of a freely falling body

summary: Instantaneous velocity is v = dx/dt (slope of the tangent to the x–t graph); acceleration is a = dv/dt = v dv/dx.
On a v–t graph, slope is acceleration and area is displacement.
For uniform acceleration: v = u+at, s = ut + (1)/(2)at^2, v^2 = u^2+2as, sn = u + (a)/(2)(2n-1).
Free fall is uniform acceleration with a = -g (upward positive). Time up equals time down; the landing speed equals the launch speed.
Projectile motion = uniform horizontal motion + free vertical fall. The path is a parabola, T = 2usinθ/g, H = u^2sin^2θ/2g, R = u^2sin 2θ/g.
Range is maximum at 45^°; complementary angles give equal ranges; the speed at the top is ucosθ, not zero.

units.title: Dynamics
topics: Solid friction: Laws of solid friction and their verifications

sections.title: Solid friction: Laws of solid friction and their verifications

summary: p = mv (kg m s⁻¹, [MLT^-1]); F = dp/dt, becoming F = ma only for constant mass.
Impulse J = FΔ t = intFdt = mv - mu, the area under the F–t graph; a longer Δ t means a smaller Fav.
m1u1 + m2u2 = m1v1 + m2v2: momentum of an isolated system is conserved — recoil, explosions, rocket propulsion.
Atwood: a = (m1-m2)g/(m1+m2), T = 2m1m2g/(m1+m2); apparent weight in a lift is m(g ± a), zero in free fall.
Torque τ = rFsinθ = rtimesF (N m); a couple has moment F × d about every point.
Equilibrium needs sumF = 0 and Στ = 0 (principle of moments).
Friction: flimiting = μs N, fk = μk N, μk < μs, independent of apparent area, and μs = tanθ = tanλ.

units.title: Work, energy and power
topics: Work done by a constant force and a variable force
Work-energy theorem; Kinetic and potential energy

sections.title: Work done by a constant force and a variable force
Work–energy theorem; kinetic and potential energy

summary: Work by a constant force: W = Fscosθ = Fcdots, a scalar in joules. Zero when the force is perpendicular to the displacement.
Work by a variable force: W = ∫ F dx = area under the F–x graph. For a spring, W = (1)/(2)kx^2.
Power P = W/t = Fcdotv; 1 hp = 746 W and 1 kW h = 3.6× 10^6 J.
Work–energy theorem: Wnet = Δ K, with K = (1)/(2)mv^2 = p^2/2m.
Potential energy: U = mgh (gravitational), U = (1)/(2)kx^2 (elastic).
Conservation of energy: K + U is constant when only conservative forces act; otherwise Wnc = Δ K + Δ U.
Conservative forces do path-independent work and zero work round a closed loop; friction and drag do not.
All collisions conserve momentum. Elastic ones also conserve kinetic energy and give u1 - u2 = v2 - v1; perfectly inelastic ones lose (1)/(2)(m1m2)/(m1+m2)(u1-u2)^2.
terms: Work done by a constant force

units.title: Circular Motion
topics: Relation between angular and linear velocity and acceleration

sections.title: Relation between angular and linear velocity and acceleration

summary: θ = s/r in radians; ω = dθ/dt = 2π/T = 2π f; α = dω/dt. Angular kinematic equations mirror the linear ones.
v = rω and at = rα; all points of a rigid rotating body share ω but not v.
Centripetal acceleration ac = v^2/r = rω^2 = 4π^2r/T^2, directed towards the centre. Total acceleration = √ac^2 + at^2.
Centripetal force Fc = mv^2/r is supplied by tension, friction, gravity or a component of the normal reaction. Centrifugal force is a fictitious force.
Conical pendulum: tanθ = v^2/rg, T = mg/cosθ, period Tp = 2π√Lcosθ/g = 2π√h/g.
Vertical circle: vtop(min) = √gr, vbottom(min) = √5gr, v2^2 = v1^2 + 4gr, and T2 - T1 = 6mg always.
Banking: tanθ = v^2/rg, independent of mass; vmax = √rg(μ+tanθ)/(1-μtanθ); on a level road vmax = √μ rg.

units.title: Gravitation
topics: Variation in value of 'g' due to altitude and depth
Centre of mass and centre of gravity
Motion of a satellite: orbital velocity and time period
Potential and kinetic energy of the satellite

sections.title: Variation in the value of g due to altitude and depth
Centre of mass and centre of gravity
Motion of a satellite: orbital velocity and time period
Potential and kinetic energy of the satellite

summary: Newton's law: F = Gm1m2/r^2 with G = 6.67×10^-11 N m^2 kg^-2; forces are an action–reaction pair, independent of the medium.
Field strength E = GM/r^2 (a vector, N kg⁻¹); at the surface g = GM/R^2, from which M = gR^2/G.
Potential V = -GM/r (a scalar, J kg⁻¹) and potential energy U = -GMm/r; E = -dV/dr, and Δ U ≈ mgh near the surface.
Altitude: gh = g(R/(R+h))^2 ≈ g(1-2h/R). Depth: gd = g(1-d/R), zero at the centre.
Centre of mass xcm = Σ mixi/Σ mi; it coincides with the centre of gravity only in a uniform field.
Orbit: vo = √GM/r, T = 2π√r^3/GM, hence T^2 ∝ r^3 (Kepler's third law).
Escape velocity ve = √2GM/R = √2gR = √2 vo = 11.2 km s^-1 for the Earth; independent of mass and direction.
Satellite energies: K = GMm/2r, U = -GMm/r, E = -GMm/2r = -K; binding energy = GMm/2r.
terms: Centre of mass and centre of gravity

units.title: Elasticity
topics: Elastic modulus: Young modulus, bulk modulus, shear modulus

sections.title: Elastic modulus: Young modulus, bulk modulus, shear modulus

summary: Hooke's law: within the elastic limit F = kx, where the force constant k = F/x (N m⁻¹). For a wire k = YA/L, so k depends on shape as well as material.
Stress = F/A (Pa, [ML^-1T^-2]); strain = change ÷ original value (no unit). Modulus = stress ÷ strain.
The stress–strain curve runs: proportional limit P, elastic limit E, yield point Y, ultimate stress U, breaking point B. Ductile materials have a long Y–B stretch; brittle ones break just after E.
Young modulus Y = FL/Ae; bulk modulus B = -pV/Δ V with compressibility K = 1/B; shear modulus η = F/(Aθ) with θ = x/L. Only B applies to liquids and gases.
Poisson's ratio σ = (Δ d/d)÷(e/L); no unit, theoretical range -1 to 0.5, real materials 0.2–0.4. Also Δ V/V = (1-2σ)e/L.
Elastic potential energy U = (1)/(2)Fe = (1)/(2)dfracYAe^2L, and energy per unit volume u = (1)/(2)× stress × strain = (1)/(2)Yvarepsilon^2.
Breaking force depends on the area of cross-section, never on the length.

units.title: Heat and Temperature
topics: Molecular concept of thermal energy, heat and temperature; cause and direction of heat flow
Thermal equilibrium and Zeroth law of thermodynamics
Thermal equilibrium as working principle of mercury thermometer

sections.title: Molecular concept of thermal energy, heat and temperature; cause and direction of heat flow
Thermal equilibrium and Zeroth law of thermodynamics
Thermal equilibrium as working principle of mercury thermometer

summary: Internal energy is the total kinetic + potential energy of the molecules; thermal energy is its temperature-dependent (kinetic) part.
Temperature measures the average molecular kinetic energy: Ek = (3)/(2)kBT with kB = 1.38×10^-23 J K^-1.
Heat is energy in transit due to a temperature difference. Its cause is the temperature difference and its direction is always hot → cold.
Thermal equilibrium is the state of zero net heat flow, reached when the two temperatures become equal.
Zeroth law: if A and B are each in equilibrium with C, they are in equilibrium with each other. This is what makes temperature measurable.
A mercury thermometer works by coming into thermal equilibrium with the body; its thermometric property is the length of the mercury thread, and t = dfraclt-l0l100-l0×100 ^°C.
Scale conversion: dfracC100 = dfracF-32180 = dfracK-273.15100.

units.title: Thermal Expansion
topics: Cubical expansion, superficial expansion and relation with linear expansion
Dulong and Petit method of determining expansivity of liquid

sections.title: Cubical expansion, superficial expansion and relation with linear expansion
Dulong and Petit method of determining expansivity of liquid

summary: Linear expansivity α = dfracl2-l1l1Δθ, so l2 = l1(1+αΔθ); unit K⁻¹.
Pullinger's apparatus measures α: rod in a steam jacket, expansion read on a micrometer screw that completes a bell circuit; α = δ l / (l1Δθ).
A2 = A1(1+βΔθ) and V2 = V1(1+γΔθ), with β = 2α, γ = 3α and α:β:γ = 1:2:3.
A cavity or hole expands exactly as if it were filled with the surrounding material.
A liquid has two expansivities: real γr and apparent γa, with γr = γa + γg where γg = 3αg for the vessel. By the weight thermometer, γa = m/[(M-m)Δθ].
Water expands anomalously: it contracts from 0 to 4 ^°C and has maximum density at 4 ^°C.
Dulong and Petit: balancing columns give hθ = h0(1+γθ), so γr = (hθ-h0)/(h0θ), with no correction for the vessel.

units.title: Quantity of Heat
topics: Measurement of specific heat capacity of solids and liquids
Specific latent heat of fusion and vaporization
Measurement of specific latent heat of fusion and vaporization

sections.title: Measurement of specific heat capacity of solids and liquids
Specific latent heat of fusion and vaporization
Measurement of specific latent heat of fusion and vaporization

summary: Heat to change temperature: Q = mcΔθ; heat capacity C = mc; water equivalent W = mc/cw.
Newton's law of cooling: dQ/dt = -K(θ-θ0), hence θ = θ0 + (θ1-θ0)e^-kt. Valid only for small excess temperature and unchanged surroundings.
Working form for problems: (θ1-θ2)/t = k[(θ1+θ2)/2 - θ0].
Specific heat capacity is measured by the method of mixtures, mscs(θs-θ2) = (mwcw+mccc)(θ2-θ1), or electrically, VIt = (mlcl+mccc)Δθ.
Latent heat is absorbed at constant temperature during a phase change: Q = mL. For water Lf = 3.34×10^5 and Lv = 2.26×10^6 J kg^-1.
Lf is measured with dried ice and Lv with dry steam from a steam trap; both use the same energy balance.
The triple point is the unique (p,T) at which solid, liquid and vapour coexist. For water: 273.16 K and 611.66 Pa.

units.title: Rate of heat flow
summary: Steady conduction: H = kA(θ1-θ2)/L = -kA dθ/dx; thermal conductivity k is in W m⁻¹ K⁻¹.
Thermal resistance R = L/(kA); resistances of slabs in series add, and H = Δθ/R.
Searle's method measures k for good conductors: k = mcw(θ4-θ3)x/[A(θ1-θ2)t]; Lee's disc is used for bad conductors.
Convection needs a moving fluid; natural convection is driven by density differences, forced convection by a fan or pump. Newton's law of cooling is a convection law.
Radiation needs no medium. a+r+t=1; a perfect black body has a = e = 1; Kirchhoff's law says good absorbers are good emitters; Prevost's theory says emission never stops.
Black-body curves are continuous with one maximum; Wien's displacement law gives λm T = 2.898×10^-3 m K.
Stefan-Boltzmann law: E = σ T^4 with σ = 5.67×10^-8 W m^-2K^-4; net loss P = eσ A(T^4-T0^4), with T in kelvin.

units.title: Ideal gas
topics: Kinetic-molecular model of an ideal gas
Derivation of pressure exerted by gas
Average translational kinetic energy of gas molecule
Boltzmann constant; root mean square speed

sections.title: Kinetic-molecular model of an ideal gas
Derivation of pressure exerted by gas
Average translational kinetic energy of gas molecule
Boltzmann constant; root mean square speed

summary: Gas laws combine into the ideal gas equation pV = nRT = NkT, with R = 8.314 J mol^-1K^-1 and T in kelvin.
Kinetic theory assumes many identical molecules of negligible volume in random motion, with no forces except during elastic collisions.
Pressure of an ideal gas: p = (1)/(3)ρoverlinec^2, equivalently pV = (1)/(3)mNoverlinec^2.
Average translational kinetic energy per molecule is E = (1)/(2)moverlinec^2 = (3)/(2)kT, and per mole (3)/(2)RT — independent of the nature of the gas.
Boltzmann constant k = R/NA = 1.38×10^-23 J K^-1.
Root mean square speed crms = √3RT/M = √3kT/m = √3p/ρ, so crms∝√T and crms∝ 1/√M.
Mayer's relation Cp - Cv = R; γ = 1.67 for monatomic and 1.40 for diatomic gases.
Dulong and Petit: the molar heat capacity of a simple solid is about 3R = 25 J mol^-1K^-1.

units.title: Reflection at curved mirror
summary: For a spherical mirror the pole P, centre of curvature C and focus F lie on the principal axis, and f = R/2 (derived from the paraxial approximation).

A real image is formed where reflected rays actually meet; it can be caught on a screen and is inverted. A virtual image is formed where the backward extensions meet; it cannot be caught on a screen and is erect.
New Cartesian convention: distances from P, positive along the incident light. Concave f<0, convex f>0; real image v<0, virtual image v>0.
Mirror formula: dfrac1v + dfrac1u = dfrac1f = dfrac2R.
Magnification: m = dfrachiho = -dfracvu = dfracf-vf = dfracff-u. Negative m = inverted and real; positive m = erect and virtual.
A concave mirror gives a real image for every object beyond F, and a magnified virtual image only when the object is between F and P.
A convex mirror gives a virtual, erect, diminished image for every position of a real object.

units.title: Refraction at plane surfaces
summary: Laws of refraction: incident ray, refracted ray and normal are coplanar; and dfracsin isin r = 1n2 (Snell's law), usually written n1sin i = n2sin r.
Absolute refractive index n = c/v; also 1n2 = n2/n1 = v1/v2 = λ1/λ2. Frequency never changes on refraction.
Reversibility gives 1n2 = 1/2n1, and the chain rule gives 1n2 × 2n3 × 3n1 = 1.
n = dfracreal depthapparent depth for near-normal viewing; apparent shift = t(1 - 1/n), and layers add: apparent depth = Σ ti/ni.
A parallel-sided slab leaves the direction unchanged but displaces the ray laterally by d = dfractsin(i-r)cos r, which is zero at normal incidence.
Total internal reflection needs light going denser → rarer with i > C, where sin C = n2/n1, or sin C = 1/n against air.
Optical fibres, totally reflecting prisms, mirages and the sparkle of diamond are all total internal reflection.
terms: Critical angle and total internal reflection

units.title: Refraction through prisms
topics: Relation between angle of prism, minimum deviation and refractive index

sections.title: Relation between angle of prism, minimum deviation and refractive index

summary: For a prism of refracting angle A: A = r1 + r2 and δ = i1 + i2 - A.
The graph of δ against i1 has one minimum. Above the minimum, two angles of incidence give the same deviation; at the minimum they coincide.
At minimum deviation the passage is symmetrical: i1 = i2, r1 = r2 = A/2, and the internal ray is parallel to the base.
Prism formula: n = dfracsinleft((A+δm)/(2)right)sinleft((A)/(2)right), with i = dfracA+δm2 at minimum deviation.
Light can emerge through the second face only if A ≤ 2C, where C is the critical angle; otherwise total internal reflection occurs inside the prism.
For a thin prism, δ = (n-1)A, independent of the angle of incidence, and thin-prism deviations simply add.

units.title: Lenses
summary: Thin lens formula dfrac1v - dfrac1u = dfrac1f with linear magnification m = hi/ho = v/u, in the New Cartesian convention.
A convex lens gives a real inverted image for any object beyond F1, and a virtual magnified one inside F1; a concave lens always gives a virtual, erect, diminished image.
Angular magnification M = β/α. For a simple microscope, M = 1 + D/f (image at the near point) and M = D/f (image at infinity), with D = 25 cm.
Refraction at one spherical surface: dfracn2v - dfracn1u = dfracn2-n1R.
Lens maker's formula: dfrac1f = (n-1)left(dfrac1R1-dfrac1R2right); in a medium, replace n by nl/nm.
Power P = 1/f (f in metres), unit dioptre; convex positive, concave negative.
Lenses in contact: dfrac1F = dfrac1f1+dfrac1f2, i.e. P = P1+P2 and m = m1m2; separated by d, P = P1+P2-dP1P2.

units.title: Dispersion
summary: Dispersion happens because n depends on wavelength, with nV > nR; for a thin prism δ = (n-1)A.
Angular dispersion θ = (nV-nR)A; mean deviation δY = (nY-1)A.
Dispersive power ω = dfracnV-nRnY-1 — dimensionless, a property of the material only. Flint glass has roughly twice the ω of crown glass.
A pure spectrum needs a narrow slit, a parallel incident beam, the prism at minimum deviation, and a lens focusing each colour separately on the screen.
Chromatic aberration: fV < fR; longitudinal chromatic aberration = ω f. Spherical aberration: marginal rays focus nearer than paraxial rays, leaving a circle of least confusion.
Condition for achromatism of two thin lenses in contact: dfracω1f1 + dfracω2f2 = 0, so one lens must be convex (crown) and the other concave (flint).
Prism pairs: (nV-nR)A + (n'V-n'R)A' = 0 gives deviation without dispersion; (nY-1)A + (n'Y-1)A' = 0 gives dispersion without deviation.

units.title: Electric Charges
topics: Coulomb's law - Force between two point charges

sections.title: Coulomb's law — force between two point charges

summary: Charge is quantised (q = ± ne, e = 1.6×10^-19 C), conserved, additive and independent of speed. Charging transfers electrons only.
1 C = 1 A s = 6.25×10^18 electronic charges.
Charging by induction gives a charge opposite to the inducing charge; the earth connection must be broken before the rod is taken away.
Coulomb's law: F = dfrac14πvarepsilon0dfracq1q2r^2 with dfrac14πvarepsilon0 = 9×10^9 N m^2C^-2 and varepsilon0 = 8.85×10^-12 C^2N^-1m^-2.
In a medium the force is reduced: Fmed = Fvac/varepsilonr.
Vector form F21 = dfrac14πvarepsilon0dfracq1q2r^2r21; the forces obey Newton's third law.
Superposition: the resultant force is the vector sum of the individual pairwise forces, F1 = Σj F1j; combine two forces with F = √Fa^2+Fb^2+2FaFbcosθ.
terms: The coulomb, defined from Coulomb's law

units.title: Electric field
topics: Electric field due to point charges; Field lines
Application of Gauss law: field of a charged sphere, line charge, charged plane conductor

sections.title: Electric field due to point charges; Field lines
Application of Gauss law: field of a charged sphere, line charge, charged plane conductor

summary: E = F/q0, measured in N C⁻¹ = V m⁻¹; for a point charge E = kQ/r^2 with k = 1/4πvarepsilon0 = 9×10^9 SI units.
Fields superpose vectorially: E = Σ Ei.
Field lines run from + to -, never cross, are densest where E is largest, meet conductors at right angles and do not exist inside a conductor.
Electric flux PhiE = EAcosθ, a scalar with unit N m² C⁻¹.
Gauss's law: oint E· dA = qenc/varepsilon0; only enclosed charge contributes.
Charged conducting sphere: E = kQ/r^2 outside, σ/varepsilon0 at the surface, 0 inside.
Long line charge: E = λ/2πvarepsilon0 r (falls as 1/r).
Charged conductor surface: E = σ/varepsilon0; thin non-conducting sheet: E = σ/2varepsilon0. Both are uniform.

units.title: Potential, potential difference and potential energy
topics: Potential difference, Potential due to a point charge, potential energy, electron volt

sections.title: Potential difference, Potential due to a point charge, potential energy, electron volt

summary: Potential difference VB - VA = WAB/q, in volts (J C⁻¹); absolute potential takes V = 0 at infinity.
Point charge: V = kQ/r — a scalar that carries the sign of the charge, so potentials add algebraically.
Potential energy: U = qV; for a pair of charges U = kq1q2/r; for a system add over all pairs.
1 eV = 1.6×10^-19 J — a unit of energy, not of potential.
An equipotential surface has constant V: no work is done moving a charge on it, and it is everywhere perpendicular to the field lines.
Conductors in equilibrium are equipotential volumes; field lines meet their surfaces at right angles.
E = -dV/dx: the field is the negative potential gradient, measured in V m⁻¹ = N C⁻¹. For parallel plates, E = V/d.

units.title: Capacitor
topics: Effect of a dielectric: Polarization and displacement

sections.title: Effect of a dielectric: Polarization and displacement

summary: C = Q/V, unit farad (C V⁻¹); capacitance depends on geometry and medium only.
Isolated sphere: C = 4πvarepsilon0R.
Parallel plate capacitor: E = σ/varepsilon0, V = Ed, and C = varepsilon0varepsilonr A/d. With a partial slab, C = varepsilon0A/(d - t + t/varepsilonr).
Series: same Q, 1/Ceq = Σ 1/Ci, result smaller than the smallest. Parallel: same V, Ceq = Σ Ci, result larger than the largest.
Stored energy U = fracQ^22C = (1)/(2)QV = (1)/(2)CV^2; it is the area under the Q–V line.
Energy per unit volume of any electric field: u = (1)/(2)varepsilon0E^2.
Sharing charge always wastes energy: Δ U = C1C2(V1-V2)^2/2(C1+C2).

A dielectric polarizes, producing bound surface charge σp = P which reduces the field to E0/varepsilonr and multiplies C by varepsilonr. Displacement D = varepsilon0E + P responds to free charge only.

units.title: DC Circuits
topics: Electric Currents; Drift velocity and its relation with current
Ohm's law, Electrical Resistance, Resistivity, Conductivity
Current-voltage relations: Ohmic and Non-Ohmic resistance
Electromotive force of a source, internal resistance
Work and power in electrical circuits

sections.title: Electric Currents; Drift velocity and its relation with current
Ohm's law, Electrical Resistance, Resistivity, Conductivity
Current-voltage relations: Ohmic and Non-Ohmic resistance
Electromotive force of a source, internal resistance
Work and power in electrical circuits

summary: Current is I = dQ/dt; in a metal I = nAvde and J = I/A = nevd, with a drift velocity of order 10^-4 m s^-1.
Ohm's law: V = IR at constant temperature. R = ρ l/A, σ = 1/ρ, and microscopically ρ = m/(ne^2τ).
Ohmic conductors give a straight I–V line through the origin; lamps, diodes and thermistors are non-ohmic.
Series: Req = R1+R2+R3. Parallel: 1/Req = 1/R1+1/R2+1/R3.
Kirchhoff: Σ I = 0 at a junction (charge conservation); Σ E = Σ IR round a loop (energy conservation).
Wheatstone bridge balances when P/Q = R/S; the metre bridge form is X = Rl/(100-l).
Galvanometer to ammeter: shunt S = IgG/(I-Ig) in parallel. To voltmeter: multiplier R = V/Ig - G in series.
Potential divider: Vout = VinR2/(R1+R2). Potentiometer: E = kl, E1/E2 = l1/l2, and r = R(l1-l2)/l2.

units.title: Nuclear physics
topics: Nuclear density, Mass number, Atomic number
Mass defect, packing fraction, BE per nucleon
Nuclear fission and fusion; energy released

sections.title: Nuclear density, Mass number, Atomic number
Mass defect, packing fraction, BE per nucleon
Nuclear fission and fusion; energy released

summary: Rutherford's alpha-scattering experiment showed the atom is mostly empty with a tiny, massive, positively charged nucleus of radius about 10^-14 m.
Z = number of protons, A = number of nucleons, N = A - Z; R = R0A^1/3 with R0 = 1.2 fm, so nuclear density is constant at about 2.3×10^17 kg m^-3.
1 u = 1.6605×10^-27 kg = 931.5 MeV. Isotopes have the same Z and different A.
Mass varies with speed, m = m0/√1-v^2/c^2; from this and dEk = v d(mv) follows Ek = (m-m0)c^2 and hence E = mc^2. A mass defect in u times 931.5 gives the energy in MeV.
Mass defect Δ m = [Zmp + (A-Z)mn] - M; binding energy B = Δ mc^2; packing fraction f = (M-A)/A.
The B/A curve peaks at about 8.8 MeV near A = 56; light nuclei release energy by fusion, heavy nuclei by fission.
Pair production needs E ≥ 1.02 MeV and a nearby nucleus; annihilation of e⁻ and e⁺ gives two 0.511 MeV photons.

Fission of ²³⁵U releases about 200 MeV (read off the B/A curve as 236×(8.5-7.6)) and 2–3 neutrons, which sustain a chain reaction above the critical mass (≈ 52 kg for bare ²³⁵U). A reactor holds the multiplication factor at k = 1 using a moderator to slow neutrons and control rods to absorb them.
terms: Chain reaction, multiplication factor and critical mass

units.title: Solids
topics: Difference between metals, insulators and semi-conductors using band theory

sections.title: Difference between metals, insulators and semi-conductors using band theory

summary: Bringing N atoms together splits each sharp atomic level into N levels so close (sim 10^-29 eV apart) that they form a continuous energy band; between bands lie forbidden gaps.
The valence band is the highest band filled at 0 K; the conduction band is the empty band above it; their separation is Eg.
A completely filled band carries no current. Conduction needs empty states just above occupied ones.
Conductor: bands overlap, Eg = 0. Semiconductor: Eg ≤ 3 eV (Ge 0.7 eV, Si 1.1 eV). Insulator: Eg > 3 eV (diamond 5.47 eV).
Semiconductors have a negative temperature coefficient of resistance because carrier number grows like e^-Eg/2kT.
Intrinsic: ne = nh = ni, and σ = e(neμe + nhμh) reduces to σi = e ni(μe+μh), with ρ = 1/σ.

Extrinsic: a pentavalent dopant makes four bonds and leaves one spare electron (n-type, donor level below CB, electrons majority); a trivalent dopant makes three bonds and leaves one hole (p-type, acceptor level above VB, holes majority). Both crystals remain electrically neutral.
Law of mass action: ne nh = ni^2 at a given temperature.

units.title: Recent Trends in physics
topics: Particle physics: Particles and antiparticles, Quarks (baryons and mesons), leptons (neutrinos)
Universe: Big Bang and Hubble law, expansion of the Universe, Dark matter, Black Hole, gravitational wave
summary: Every particle has an antiparticle of equal mass and opposite charge. Pair production needs ≥ 1.02 MeV; annihilation of e^-e^+ gives two 0.511 MeV photons.
Quarks come in six flavours: u, c, t with charge +(2)/(3)e and d, s, b with -(1)/(3)e. Baryons are qqq (p = uud, n = udd); mesons are qq (π^+ = ud). Free quarks are never seen.
The six leptons are e, μ, τ and their neutrinos. Neutrinos are neutral, feel only the weak force, and oscillate between flavours — proof of tiny mass.
Hubble's law v = H0 d with H0 ≈ 70 km s^-1Mpc^-1; the Hubble time 1/H0 ≈ 14 billion years.
Big Bang evidence: the expansion, the 2.725 K cosmic microwave background, and the 75% H / 25% He abundance. Age = 13.8 billion years.
Space itself expands, with no centre, and ever faster: the universe is 68% dark energy, 27% dark matter, 5% ordinary matter.
Dark matter is inferred from flat rotation curves, cluster dynamics and lensing; it has never been detected directly. Newtonian orbits give v = √GM(r)/r, so a flat curve means M(r) ∝ r.
Black hole: escape velocity exceeds c; event horizon at Rs = 2GM/c^2. Imaged by the Event Horizon Telescope (M87\* 2019, Sgr A\* 2022).
